The Unified Payments Interface, launched in 2016 as a modest experiment in interoperable digital transfers, has since grown into the backbone of the country's retail economy, processing billions of transactions every month. This proliferation of real-time payments has been driven less by any single innovation than by a confluence of factors: affordable smartphones, cheap mobile data, and a regulatory framework willing to experiment with open, shared infrastructure rather than leaving the market to a handful of proprietary players.

Millions of households that once operated entirely in cash now hold bank accounts linked to mobile numbers, allowing them to receive government subsidies, insurance payouts, and wages without the delays and leakages that plagued earlier disbursement systems. Regulators have responded with tighter transaction limits for new payees, mandatory cooling-off periods for large transfers, and public awareness campaigns, but enforcement varies widely across states and remains an unfinished project.
